findings.issue: Source: “so great a minister of fear was he whom they had lost”; candidate adds “a great source of terror to the enemy”, a qualifier the source does not state.
findings.fix: They all broke into a wail, and Achilles led their lament. Three times they drove their chariots around the body in sorrow, and Thetis stirred a deeper longing to weep in every one of them. The sand of the shore and the men’s armor were wet with tears, so great a source of fear was the man they had lost. The son of Peleus mourned above them all. He laid his blood-stained hand on his friend’s chest and cried out: “Farewell, Patroclus, even in the house of Hades. Now I will do everything I promised you earlier. I will drag Hector here and let the dogs eat him raw. And before your pyre I will kill twelve noble sons of the Trojans, to avenge you.”

findings.issue: Source “the fleet descendant of Aeacus”; STYLE-NOTE renders plain “fleet” as “swift” (swift-footed is for “fleet of foot”), candidate has “swift-footed descendant of Aeacus”.
findings.fix: With these words he treated the body of noble Hector shamefully, stretching it out in the dust beside the bier of Patroclus. Then the others took off their armor, unhitched the horses from their chariots, and sat down in a great crowd beside the ship of the swift descendant of Aeacus. He gave them a rich funeral feast. They slaughtered and cut up many fine oxen, and many sheep and bleating goats. They also singed many fat, well-fed tusked boars and set them to roast in the flames of Hephaestus. Streams of blood ran all around the place where the body lay.

findings.issue: Source: the spirit “vanished as a vapour”; candidate has “vanished like smoke”, changing the image.
findings.fix: He stretched out his arms toward the spirit as he spoke and tried to hold it, but there was nothing there. The spirit vanished like vapor, gibbering and whining, into the earth. Achilles sprang to his feet and struck his hands together. He cried out in grief: “It is true, then. Even in the house of Hades there are ghosts and phantoms with no life in them. All night long the sad spirit of Patroclus has hovered over my head, moaning pitifully, telling me what I must do for him, and looking amazingly like himself.”

findings.issue: Source “swart iron” (dark iron); candidate “gray iron” changes the quality.
findings.fix: So he spoke, and they obeyed the son of Peleus. First they poured red wine on the thick layer of ashes and put out the fire. With many tears they picked out the whitened bones of their beloved comrade and laid them in a golden urn in two layers of fat. They covered the urn with a linen cloth and took it inside the tent. They marked out the circle for the mound, laid a foundation for it around the pyre, and at once heaped up the earth. When they had raised the mound, they were going away, but Achilles kept the people there and made them sit in assembly. He brought prizes from the ships: cauldrons, tripods, horses and mules, noble oxen, women with fair girdles, and dark iron.

findings.issue: Source: “as an heirloom and memorial of the funeral of Patroclus”; candidate “to keep in memory of the funeral” drops the heirloom.
findings.fix: With that he handed the mare to Noemon, the comrade of Antilochus, and took the cauldron for himself. Meriones had come in fourth, and he carried off the two talents of gold. The fifth prize, the two-handled urn, was still unclaimed, so Achilles gave it to Nestor. He went up to the old man among the gathered Argives and said, “Take this, my good old friend, as an heirloom and a memorial of the funeral of Patroclus, for you will not see him again among the Argives. I give you this prize though you cannot win one. You can no longer wrestle or fight, you cannot enter the javelin match or the foot races, because age has laid its heavy hand on you.”

findings.issue: Source “Thus did they make their moan throughout the city”; candidate resolves to “the Trojans ... their city”. Supported by the end of Book 22, acceptable.
